blocks.text: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a central nervous system (CNS) disorder characterised by the degeneration of oligodendrocytes, which are responsible for forming myelin sheaths around nerve fibres.

Loss of myelin leads to leakage of K+ through voltage-gated channels, which in turn leads to hyperpolarisation or abnormal depolarisation, impaired nerve signal conduction, and symptoms such as paraparesis, paresthesia, optic neuritis, dysarthria, and dysphagia.

blocks.text: **Microglia (Option A):** are non-neural cells that act like scavenger cells and remove debris formed by infection, injury, and disease; they have no role in myelination.

Rubbing or shaking an injured area decreases the pain due to the injury. This is due to simultaneous activation of innocuous cutaneous mechanoreceptors thereby reducing pain by affecting dorsal horn neuron responsiveness. This is called the gate-control mechanism of pain modulation.
**Gate control theory:** Developed By Patrick David Wall and Ronald Melzack It suggests that pain perception is influenced by the interaction of different nerve fibers in the spinal cord.
Large-diameter Aα and Aβ fibers inhibit pain signals from C fibers in the dorsal horn of spinal cord by activating inhibitory interneurons, effectively "closing the gate". (Option C, D ruled out)
When small-diameter fibers are more active, they "open the gate," allowing pain signals to reach the brain.
**Influencing Factors:** Psychological factors, including cognitive and emotional states affect gate control.

items.text: Depression can keep the gate open more often, increasing pain perception
Unhealthy lifestyles can also result in open gates.

blocks.text: **Application:** According to the gate-control theory, electrical stimulation of large nerve fibers should inhibit pain induced by C fibers alone.
Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS) uses electrodes to activate Aa and Aß fibers near the injury, thereby using the gate-control mechanism for pain relief.

The human hand contains four types of mechanoreceptors that work together to sense contact with objects:

items.text: **Merkel cells and Ruffini endings:** Activate for steady pressure.
**Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles:** Activate for tingling and vibratory sensations.

blocks.text: Location of a stimulus is encoded by spatial distribution of the population of receptors activated.

A receptor fires only when the skin close to its sensory terminals is touched. The receptive fields of mechanoreceptors (shown as red areas on fingertips) differ in size and response to touch. Merkel cells and Meissner corpuscles provide the most precise localization as they have the smallest receptive fields and are most sensitive to pressure applied by a small probe.

Stimulus intensity is signaled by firing rates of individual receptors; duration of stimulus is signaled by time course of firing. The spike trains indicate action potentials elicited by pressure from a small probe at the center of each receptive field.
Meissner and Pacinian corpuscles adapt rapidly, the others adapt slowly
**Accommodation:** Refers to a gradual increase in threshold caused by prolonged slowly rising sub-threshold nerve depolarization, resulting from the inactivation of sodium channels.

**Adaptation:** If a supra-threshold stimulus persists unchanged for several minutes without a change in position or amplitude, the neural response diminishes and sensation is lost, a condition called receptor adaptation.

Mass reflex is due to excessive activity in the spinal cord causing massive discharge in large portions of the cord. Mass reflex can sometimes be used to give patients with paraplegia a degree of bladder and bowel control. They can be trained to initiate urination and defecation by stroking or pinching their thighs, thus producing an intentional mass reflex.

blocks.text: The patient's history of multiple sclerosis and the presence of ankle clonus strongly suggest damage to the descending motor pathways. This damage leads to hyperactive muscle spindles and, consequently, clonus. Clonus is characterized by rhythmic muscle contractions in response to sustained stretch.
CLONUS

items.text: **Definition:** Regular, repetitive, rhythmic contractions of a muscle subjected to sudden, maintained stretch
**Cause:** Increased γ-motor neuron activity leading to hypersensitive muscle spindles
**Mechanism:** Hypersensitivity to stretch triggers rhythmic contractions
**Common Sites:** Ankle clonus initiated by brisk, maintained dorsiflexion of the foot, leading to rhythmic plantar flexion
**Associated Conditions:**
Damage to descending motor pathways
Traumatic brain injury
Brain tumors
Strokes
Multiple sclerosis
Spinal cord injury
**Renshaw Cells:**
Inhibitory interneurons receiving excitatory input from α-motor neurons
Damage leads to loss of inhibitory control, contributing to clonus
**Reflexes Involved:**
Stretch reflex
Inverse stretch reflex
Interplay in hypersensitive muscle spindles contributes to clonus

blocks.text: Increased GABAergic activity (Option B) in the spinal cord would actually reduce clonus as GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter.
**Enhanced Golgi tendon organ activation (Option D):** Golgi tendon organs (GTOs) are involved in the inverse stretch reflex, which causes muscle relaxation in response to increased tension.

Inverse Stretch Reflex is activated when there is excessive tension in a muscle, as detected by the Golgi tendon organ (GTO). When the tension becomes too high, the GTO sends signals to the spinal cord, which in turn inhibits the alpha motor neurons innervating the same muscle, leading to muscle relaxation.
**Withdrawal Reflex (Option B):** is a protective mechanism that causes a body part to automatically move away from a source of pain or discomfort.
**Crossed extensor reflex (Option D):** causes the opposite limb to extend when a withdrawal reflex is initiated in one limb.
The Golgi tendon organ, when activated by excessive muscle tension, triggers a protective reflex that inhibits the contracting muscle, preventing tendon rupture or muscle tearing.

When stimulated, signals are transmitted to the spinal cord, triggering the inverse stretch reflex (also called autogenic inhibition).

The interneuron inhibits the anterior motor neuron of the respective muscle, causing relaxation, this is a bisynaptic pathway.
This protects the muscle and tendon from excessive tension that might cause tearing.

blocks.text: **Jendrassik Maneuver:** Clinical technique used to enhance the sensitivity of the stretch reflex (and thus, the response of the muscle spindle).
The maneuver involves the patient performing an isometric contraction in a muscle group distant from the one being tested.

items.text: Clenching the teeth
Locking the fingers and pulling the hands apart
Squeezing the knees together.

blocks.text: The maneuver is thought to increase γ-motor neuron activity, making the muscle spindles more sensitive to stretch.
**Alpha-Gamma Coactivation:** On voluntary muscle contraction, the brain often signals both α- and γ-motor neurons simultaneously. This is known as alpha-gamma coactivation.
Activating γ-motor neurons causes intrafusal fibers to contract, maintaining tension in the spindle ensuring that spindle remains sensitive to stretch even during voluntary contractions.

**Example:** When catching a ball, alpha-gamma coactivation keeps the muscle spindles responsive and allows for rapid adjustments to maintain grip and arm position as the weight of the ball impacts the hand.

**α-motor neuron (Option A):** While the knee-jerk reflex does involve the activation of α-motor neurons to cause the quadriceps muscle to contract, the Jendrassik maneuver does not directly activate these neurons.
**Golgi tendon organ (Option C):** the sensitivity of the Golgi tendon organ is not directly affected by the Jendrassik maneuver.
**Extrafusal muscle fibers (Option D):** are not directly activated by the Jendrassik maneuver.
Stretch reflex pathway: Regulates muscle length and contributes to postural control. It is initiated by the stretching of muscle, which activates specialised sensory receptors.
**Muscle Spindles:** Consists of intrafusal muscle fibers (nuclear bag and nuclear chain fibers), Sensory nerve endings (group Ia and II afferent fibers), and Gamma motor neuron endings

**Afferent Limb:** When a muscle is stretched, the muscle spindles are also stretched, stimulating the sensory endings. This stretch-induced stimulation generates receptor potentials that trigger action potentials in the afferent fibers.

**Integration Center:** The Ia afferent fibers, have a large diameter and, conduct action potentials, transmit signals to the spinal cord through the dorsal roots. Within the spinal cord, these fibers form direct (monosynaptic) connections with alpha motor neurons located in the anterior horn.
**Efferent Limb:** The activated alpha motor neurons send signals through axons, which exit the spinal cord and travel to the extrafusal muscle fibers.
**Effector:** The arrival of action potentials at the neuromuscular junctions causes the release of acetylcholine, initiating muscle fiber contraction.
This counteracts the initial stretch by shortening the muscle, thus restoring its original length.

Type Ia fibers are large, rapidly conducting sensory fibers that originate from the central portion of both nuclear bag and nuclear chain fibers within the muscle spindle. These fibers are responsible for transmitting information about the velocity and length of muscle stretch to the spinal cord.

items.text: **Nuclear Bag Fiber:** Respond to changes in muscle length (stretch). Two subtypes: dynamic and static.
**Dynamic Nuclear Bag Fiber:** Detects real-time shortening/lengthening of a muscle (i.e., the velocity).
**Static Nuclear Bag Fiber:** Detects sustained/maintained length of a muscle but plays no role in detecting velocity. (Option B ruled out)

**Nuclear Chain Fiber:** Thinner and shorter than nuclear bag fibers and lack a definite bag. Static response of the muscle spindle, providing information about the steady-state muscle length. (Option C ruled out)

blocks.text: Extrafusal fibers (Option D) are regular contractile fibers of skeletal muscle responsible for generating force and movement. They are not a part of the muscle spindle and do not directly contribute to the stretch reflex.
Muscle spindles are sensory receptors found within skeletal muscle. The function of a muscle spindle is to detect changes in muscle length, also called stretch.

items.text: **Regulating Muscle Length:** Provides feedback to regulate muscle length.
**Damping:** Smoothens muscle contractions and prevents jerkiness.
**Stabilizing Body Position:** Maintains posture and balance by informing the spinal cord and motor centers about muscle length.
**Higher Motor Control:** Information is transmitted to the cerebellum and cerebral cortex.

The periaqueductal grey (PAG) matter region in the midbrain plays a crucial role in the descending pain modulation pathway. When stimulated by opioids like morphine, PAG neurons activate neurons in the brainstem, the nucleus raphe magnus (which releases serotonin) and the rostral ventromedial medulla (which releases norepinephrine).
These neurons project to the dorsal horn, where they release their respective neurotransmitters to inhibit the activity of pain-transmitting neurons.

blocks.text: Thalamic pain syndrome typically starts within the first six months post stroke, but can develop even after ten years. It is persistent and potentially life-long pain that does not resolve.

items.text: **Definition:** Thalamic pain syndrome or Dejerine Roussy syndrome or Central post-stroke pain is a rare central neuropathic pain syndrome that occurs after infarction of the ventro-posterolateral thalamus
**Aetiology:** Vascular lesions affecting the central somatosensory system, most commonly ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke (Option B ruled out)
**Pathophysiology:** Damage to the spinothalamic tract or thalamus disrupts sensory processing, leading to abnormal pain perception (Option A ruled out)
**Epidemiology:** Prevalence ranges from 8% to 46%
**Onset:** Typically within the first six months post-stroke, but can develop after ten years also
**Symptoms:** Sharp, burning and stabbing pain with hyperalgesia and allodynia; Pain is described as pricking, aching, freezing, shooting, etc.
**Diagnosis:** Based on history, clinical examination, and imaging: CT/MRI to confirm stroke
**Treatment:**
Pharmacological: Antidepressants, Anticonvulsants, (Option D ruled out) Opioids, NMDA receptor antagonists
Non-Pharmacological: Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), Deep brain stimulation (DBS) Motor cortex stimulation
**Prognosis:** Poor Persistent and potentially life-long pain (Option C)
**Complications:**
Reduces quality of life
Depression or anxiety
Sleep disturbance
Drug dependence
Poor social interactions
Increased suicide risk

blocks.text: Slow-chronic pain can usually be localized only to a major part of the body, such as one arm or leg, but not to a specific point on the arm or leg. This phenomenon is due to the multisynaptic, diffuse connectivity of the Paleo-Spinothalamic pathway, which is why patients have difficulty localizing the source in some chronic types of pain.
